chapter: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
title: Trumpeters Shorty Baker and Ray Nance
summary: Baker was among the best, applauded at Carnegie Hall; Nance was a multi-talented violinist and singer whose A Train chorus became a model.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: We talked a little bit about Shorty (inaudible) Baker, ah, how did you feel about his playing?

I think he was one of the best of the best. He worked with us for quite awhile. His lush tone, and his beautiful way of making his passages and the things that he picked out to make in his passages, were really something terrific. He was originally with what's that girl piano player?
Mary Lou Williams and the band that

she was with, you know, and then he came with us, finally. And I remember distinctly one of his terrific things he did was on a transitional phrase, I think it was, "Black, Brown and Beige." Which he played all by himself, in no time, you know, just played and it was so terrific that at the concert in Carnegie Hall the audience gave him applause. Really applauded, very definitely, for this passage. It was beautiful, beautiful. And all through the years he did such terrific work and then he finally came with Johnny and he really helped the band there, very much.

Well Ray Nance was a triple threat, or would you call him the quadruple threat. He was a good trumpet player, he had such terrific ideas, he was a terrific violinist, he could dance, he could sing, he was just an all around musician's musician. And they still listen to his chorus on the original rendition of "A Train." That's -- they still try to pattern it after that chorus. He played. He was too much, as we say, too much.
